Pregnancy

Pubic-joint pain in pregnancy: assessment, support and recovery

Updated: November 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pain low at the front of the pelvis can make walking, turning in bed or putting on trousers surprisingly difficult. Pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain is one possible explanation, but pain in this location does not by itself identify the cause. Assessment helps distinguish a manageable joint-and-muscle problem from a less common joint separation or a condition needing urgent treatment.

The pubic joint and the meaning of SPD

The pubic symphysis is the joint joining the two pubic bones at the front of the pelvis. Together with the joints at the back, it forms part of the pelvic ring. Pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain, or PGP, may be felt at the front, back or both. The older term SPD commonly means symphysis pubis dysfunction; it does not mean that the bones have necessarily separated abnormally.

Pubic symphysis diastasis is a different diagnosis involving excessive separation of this joint. It is less common and may become apparent around childbirth with substantial pain and difficulty moving. Ordinary front-of-pelvis pain, a click or a sensation of looseness cannot distinguish dysfunction from diastasis. An examination is more useful than assuming that everyone with pain has a separated joint.

Symptoms worth describing clearly

PGP can cause pain over the pubic bone, in the groin, hips, thighs or lower back, sometimes with clicking or grinding. Walking, stairs, standing on one leg to dress, getting into a car, moving the knees apart or rolling in bed may provoke it. Note where the pain is, when it began and which activities have become difficult; the pattern helps the clinician assess it.

A new visible swelling, marked local tenderness, sudden major change in pain or inability to bear weight deserves prompt clinical assessment rather than being labelled a normal sign of SPD. A painful joint is not proof of swelling from inflammation, nor does pain intensity reliably measure the size of a joint gap. Do not repeatedly press on the area or force the legs apart to test it.

Why it happens and what risk factors can tell us

Pregnancy changes loading, posture and how the muscles and joints support the pelvis. Hormonal changes may contribute, but a simple explanation that excess relaxin loosens the joint and therefore causes every case of pain is not established. Studies relating hormone levels, measured joint width and symptoms have produced differing results; a hormone test is not a routine way to explain this pain.

Previous pelvic or back pain, pelvic injury and PGP in an earlier pregnancy can be relevant to assessment. A demanding physical job may also make symptoms harder to manage. Small studies of the separate condition diastasis have reported differing associations, including first birth or twins in particular populations. A large baby, multiple pregnancy or previous births does not predict that an individual will develop a separation, and having no risk factor does not exclude a problem.

What an assessment involves

Tell your midwife or clinician about new pelvic pain, especially when it limits walking, sleep or daily tasks. A pregnancy-experienced physiotherapist may assess posture, movement, back and hip function and the location of tenderness, while the maternity team checks for other explanations. The history includes an injury or fall, urinary symptoms, fever, bleeding, fluid loss and the baby's movements when these are normally felt.

A diagnosis of PGP is usually based on clinical assessment, not a home test or a scan for every painful pubic joint. When PGP has been assessed and confirmed, the condition itself does not harm the baby; this reassurance does not establish the cause or safety of new or unexplained pelvic pain. Sudden severe symptoms around birth, an inability to walk, a suspected injury or persistent atypical pain may require a different examination and specialist assessment for diastasis or another cause. A familiar musculoskeletal diagnosis should not be used to dismiss new warning symptoms.

Imaging is chosen for a clinical question

Ultrasound or MRI may be useful when clinicians need information that examination cannot provide, such as concern about significant joint separation or another cause of pain. They are not automatically necessary for routine PGP. The choice depends on the suspected problem, pregnancy stage, availability and whether the result would change care.

An X-ray is not absolutely forbidden during pregnancy. A necessary radiograph or another imaging test should not be withheld solely because someone is pregnant when its benefits justify its use; the team chooses the appropriate investigation and explains exposure considerations. After birth, a pelvic radiograph may be one option for suspected diastasis, but it is not automatically the best test for every patient. Ask what question the test will answer rather than requesting a scan solely to measure pain.

Physiotherapy and a support belt

Early referral can provide a practical plan for movement, pacing and exercises adapted to the painful activities. NICE recommends considering physiotherapy services for exercise advice and/or a non-rigid lumbopelvic belt. This is support for an individual care plan, not evidence that everyone needs a belt or that a belt prevents a joint from becoming damaged.

The evidence has limits: exercise studies vary in quality, and a belt trial found improved pain without a demonstrated improvement in everyday function. Ask a physiotherapist to advise on fit, when to wear it and whether it actually helps. Crutches or other aids may be appropriate when walking is difficult. Manual treatment or acupuncture should not be presented as proven cures; NICE found insufficient evidence to recommend manual therapy alone or acupuncture for this problem.

Adjusting everyday movement

Share weight evenly through both feet when standing, and sit down to put on underwear, trousers or shoes. Keep tasks within a comfortable range and avoid repeatedly standing on one leg, twisting while carrying a load or carrying a child on one hip. Change position regularly, divide demanding chores into smaller parts and ask for help with heavy lifting or repeated trips on stairs.

When getting in or out of a car or turning in bed, moving the legs together can reduce discomfort; do not force a painful position. A pillow between the knees and under the bump may make side-lying more comfortable. For a bath or shower, consider a stable seat, hand support and assistance if stepping over an edge feels unsafe. These are ways to adapt a task, not a requirement to keep the knees rigidly together throughout the day.

Activity, rest and symptom relief

Aim for manageable activity balanced with rest rather than pushing through pain or prescribing yourself bed rest. A physiotherapist can tailor pelvic-floor, abdominal or other exercises to your symptoms; there is no single stretching routine suitable for everyone with front-of-pelvis pain. Stop an activity that clearly worsens symptoms and ask how to modify it. Swimming or other water-based activity may suit some people, but painful leg movements still need adjustment.

Heat or cold and a comfortable resting position may offer short-term relief when used safely. Seek advice if sleep, caring for children or work is becoming unmanageable. Severe restriction of mobility may need stronger support, equipment or hospital assessment. Reduced mobility also changes blood-clot risk, so the maternity team may consider preventive measures; do not decide on anticoagulants yourself.

Pain medicines during pregnancy and breastfeeding

Ask your maternity team or pharmacist which pain relief is suitable for your pregnancy, medical history and other medicines. Paracetamol is usually an option during pregnancy and breastfeeding when used as directed, but check combination products to avoid taking it twice. Do not assume a medicine sold without a prescription, a supplement or a topical product is suitable simply because the pain feels muscular.

Do not start ibuprofen or another NSAID in pregnancy without medical advice. FDA guidance highlights fetal kidney and amniotic-fluid risks from around 20 weeks, with additional concerns later in pregnancy; prescribed low-dose aspirin for another indication is a different situation and should not be stopped on your own. After birth, ibuprofen or diclofenac may be suitable during breastfeeding, particularly with a full-term healthy infant, but premature or unwell infants and other medicines require individual advice. A breastfeeding recommendation is not a pregnancy recommendation.

When maternity advice should not wait

Contact your maternity service urgently for pelvic or abdominal pain with vaginal bleeding or spotting, fluid loss or unusual discharge, regular cramps or tightenings, urinary pain or a new need to pass urine frequently, or fever or feeling hot, cold or shivery. If you may be going into labour before 37 weeks, your waters break, or the baby is moving less than usual, contact the maternity team immediately, including at night. Do not wait for the next appointment or for all these signs to appear. Also seek urgent advice for pelvic pain with difficulty passing urine or stool, blood in urine or stool, nausea, or vomiting and diarrhoea. Abdominal pain with lower back pain, cloudy, pink, red or brown urine, or pain that remains after 30–60 minutes of rest needs immediate maternity contact. Do not wait to rest if an urgent or emergency warning already applies.

Seek emergency help for pelvic or abdominal pain that is severe, worsening or painful with movement or touch, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, actual fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or sudden confusion. Pregnancy bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness also needs emergency help, even if the bleeding is not heavy. These are separate warning patterns. Do not drive yourself: ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. For an already assessed stable PGP movement pattern, follow the agreed care plan; new or changed symptoms still need reassessment.

Other urgent signs: nerves and blood clots

Emergency assessment is needed for sciatica on both sides, severe or worsening weakness or numbness in both legs, new numbness around the genitals or anus, new trouble starting or controlling urination or inability to urinate, or loss of bowel sensation or control. Do not assume these are ordinary pregnancy pressure or wait for a physiotherapy appointment. The signs are alternatives, and you should not drive yourself to emergency care.

Contact a clinician immediately for a painful, tender, hot, red, swollen or newly heavy leg, particularly on one side; a clot does not require every sign or obvious swelling. Sudden unexplained breathlessness, chest pain or tightness, coughing blood, feeling very unwell or collapsing needs immediate emergency help. Do not massage a suspected clot or walk through severe unexplained symptoms. Limited mobility with pelvic pain is a reason to discuss prevention, not to dismiss these warnings.

Planning labour and birth

Most people with assessed PGP can have a vaginal birth. Tell the team about painful movements, comfortable positions and any mobility aids before labour, and ask that the legs are supported. A birth plan can record the comfortable range of movement so care does not rely on you repeatedly explaining it while in pain. Water and usual pain-relief options, including an epidural when appropriate, may be considered.

PGP alone is not normally a reason for a caesarean birth or early induction. A confirmed substantial separation, other pelvic injury or another obstetric condition needs an individual specialist plan; advice for routine PGP should not be applied automatically. The decision concerns the whole clinical situation, not the label SPD or a single measurement.

Recovery after birth and persistent pain

PGP often improves after birth, but improvement is not guaranteed within a few days or weeks. Continue suitable support and physiotherapy, gradually adjusting activity as advised. Review is important if pain persists, worsens or prevents walking or caring for yourself. It is not enough to assume that relaxin production has stopped and the joint must therefore have recovered.

Confirmed diastasis may need coordinated maternity, physiotherapy and orthopaedic care. Support, pain relief and rehabilitation are commonly used, while some patients need an operation based on their particular injury and progress. Small observational studies show variable recovery and sometimes persistent symptoms; they do not justify a universal operation threshold or timetable. New pain after a fall, fever, urinary problems or the warning signs above still needs prompt assessment during the postpartum period.

Preparing for a useful follow-up

Bring a short account of the painful location, onset, triggers, walking ability, sleep, work and childcare demands, along with any medicines and previous pelvic injuries. Ask whether the diagnosis is PGP, suspected diastasis or something else; what examination or imaging would change care; and which activities, aids and pain medicines are appropriate now.

Agree when progress will be reviewed and whom to contact if mobility deteriorates or new symptoms appear. If you had PGP in an earlier pregnancy, discussing support early can help prepare for another pregnancy, although recurrence is not inevitable. The aim is comfortable, safe function and appropriate assessment, rather than proving that the pelvis is loose or forcing a particular exercise despite pain.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Record the painful location, triggers and effect on walking, sleep and daily tasks for your clinical review.

Ask for a practical movement, physiotherapy and medicine plan, including whether an aid or selective imaging would help.

Keep the maternity team's contact details and agreed warning plan accessible; do not delay assessment to finish a symptom record.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you organise symptoms, questions and the care plan discussed with your team. It cannot diagnose PGP or joint separation, interpret a scan, select pain medicines or replace urgent assessment. A brief record is useful only when it does not delay getting help.

When to seek help

New pelvic pain in pregnancy needs clinical advice. Seek urgent maternity help for pain with bleeding, fluid loss, unusual discharge, fever or urinary symptoms, and immediately for possible preterm labour or reduced usual fetal movement. Emergency help is needed for severe/worsening or movement/touch-related pelvic or abdominal pain; pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, actual fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or sudden confusion; or pregnancy bleeding with severe pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness. New saddle numbness, bladder/bowel dysfunction or serious bilateral leg symptoms also require emergency assessment. A painful, hot, red or swollen leg needs immediate advice; sudden unexplained breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood or collapse needs emergency help. Signs are independent alternatives, not an all-required list. Do not drive yourself in an emergency or postpone care to try a belt, exercise or painkiller.

Evidence notes updated: November 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • SPD usually refers to dysfunction; pain alone does not diagnose excessive pubic-joint separation.
  • Early assessment and tailored physiotherapy can help with walking, dressing, sleep and other daily tasks.
  • Belts and exercises may help, but evidence and individual response vary; no treatment guarantees prevention of joint damage.
  • Necessary imaging is chosen according to its clinical value, not a blanket pregnancy X-ray ban.
  • New warning symptoms or severe loss of mobility need assessment, and persistent postpartum pain deserves follow-up.

Frequently asked questions

Does pain over the pubic bone mean the joint has separated?

No. PGP or symphysis pubis dysfunction can cause front-of-pelvis pain without an excessive separation. Diastasis is a distinct diagnosis requiring clinical assessment and, when appropriate, imaging. Clicking, swelling or pain intensity alone cannot establish it.

Which symptoms are typical of pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain?

Pain at the front or back of the pelvis, groin or thighs may worsen with walking, stairs, standing on one leg, turning in bed or getting into a car. Describe the pattern to a clinician. A new swelling, sudden major change or inability to bear weight needs assessment rather than automatic reassurance.

Is relaxin the cause, and who is more likely to develop pain?

The cause is multifactorial, with changes in loading, posture and muscle-joint function. Hormonal studies are mixed; one hormone does not explain every case. Previous pelvic or back pain, injury or PGP can matter. Reported risk factors for diastasis vary between small studies and cannot predict an individual's outcome.

Are an X-ray or MRI always needed?

No. Routine PGP is usually assessed clinically. Ultrasound, MRI or a radiograph may be considered for a particular question, such as suspected separation or another injury. Necessary imaging is not automatically prohibited in pregnancy; the team explains why its benefits justify its use.

Will a support belt or exercise cure it?

Neither guarantees a cure. A physiotherapist may suggest adapted exercise and a non-rigid lumbopelvic belt, checking fit and response. Keep activity manageable, sit to dress, share standing weight evenly and adapt painful bed or car movements. Do not force stretches or assume acupuncture or manual treatment alone is proven to work.

Can I take ibuprofen or other pain relief?

Ask your maternity team or pharmacist. Paracetamol is usually an option when used as directed, but duplicate ingredients and personal contraindications matter. Do not self-start NSAIDs in pregnancy, particularly from around 20 weeks. After birth, breastfeeding recommendations differ and depend on the medicine and the infant's health; follow an individual plan.

Will I need a caesarean birth, and when should the pain stop?

Most people with PGP can have a vaginal birth with supported positions; PGP alone does not normally require caesarean birth or induction. Confirmed significant separation or another condition needs individual planning. Many improve after birth, but persistent or worsening symptoms need follow-up rather than a fixed recovery promise.

When is pelvic pain an emergency?

Seek emergency help for severe or worsening pelvic/abdominal pain or pain with movement or touch; pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or sudden confusion; or pregnancy bleeding with severe pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness. New saddle numbness, bladder/bowel dysfunction or serious bilateral leg symptoms are also emergencies. Do not drive yourself. These signs are alternatives; new maternity bleeding, fluid loss, possible preterm labour or reduced usual fetal movement needs immediate maternity contact even without the emergency pattern.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
